statement: If two circles touch one another, they will not have the same centre.
heath_proof: For let the two circles ABC, CDE touch one another at the point C; I say that they will not have the same centre. For, if possible, let it be F; let FC be joined, and let FEB be drawn through at random. Then, since the point F is the centre of the circle ABC, FC is equal to FB. Again, since the point F is the centre of the circle CDE, FC is equal to FE. But FC was proved equal to FB; therefore FE is also equal to FB, the less to the greater: which is impossible. Therefore F is not the centre of the circles ABC, CDE.
ai_proof_text:
3.6
**Statement:** If two circles touch one another, they will not have the same centre.

**Step 1.** Let the two circles ABC and CDE touch one another at the point C; that is, they meet one another at C and do not cut one another (D3.3). I say that they will not have the same centre.

**Step 2.** For, if possible, let F be the centre of both circles. Then F is a point lying within the circle ABC such that all straight lines falling from F upon the circumference of ABC are equal to one another; and likewise F is a point lying within the circle CDE such that all straight lines falling from F upon the circumference of CDE are equal to one another (D1.15, D1.16).

**Step 3.** Join FC (P1). Since C is on the circumference of ABC and F is the centre of ABC, FC is a straight line falling from the centre upon the circumference of ABC; and since C is also on the circumference of CDE and F is the centre of CDE, FC is likewise a straight line falling from the centre upon the circumference of CDE.

**Step 4.** Since ABC and CDE are two circles and not one and the same circle, their circumferences do not wholly coincide; let E be a point on the circumference of one of them, say CDE, which does not lie on the circumference of the other, ABC.

**Step 5.** Join FE (P1). Because F lies within the circle ABC (Step 2), the straight line FE, produced if necessary (P2), meets the circumference of ABC; let it meet it at B. Since E is not on the circumference of ABC (Step 4), E and B are distinct points, and both lie on the same straight line drawn from F and on the same side of F. Hence either E lies between F and B, so that FE is a part of FB, or B lies between F and E, so that FB is a part of FE.

**Step 6.** Since F is the centre of CDE and both C and E are on its circumference, FE is equal to FC (D1.15). Since F is the centre of ABC and both C and B are on its circumference, FB is equal to FC (D1.15).

**Step 7.** Therefore FE is equal to FB, each being equal to the same straight line FC (CN1).

**Step 8.** But by Step 5 one of FE, FB is a part of the other, and the whole is greater than the part (CN5); so the less would be equal to the greater, which is impossible.

**Step 9.** Therefore F is not the centre of both circles. Hence the two circles ABC and CDE which touch one another do not have the same centre. Q.E.D.
